extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy of science / scientifically literate public
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook/chapter-style exposition on the nature of space (and relatedly time), distinguishing perceptual (real) space from conceptual (ideal) space and giving criteria for the scientific validity and usefulness of concepts (points, lines, continuity, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Space as a mode of the perceptive faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Space is a mode of the perceptive faculty; it is peculiar to the individual perceptive faculty and is not an attribute of the unknowable world behind sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without any perceptive faculty sensations might exist but there could not be that mode of perception we term space. Space is not in phenomena but is our mode of perceiving them; treat space as a feature of consciousness rather than an objective container.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of perceptual spaces across humans
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of coexisting phenomena is apparently the same, at any rate, for the vast majority of human perceptive faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ask 'why space seems the same to you and me' but rather 'why your space and my space are alike.' Social and evolutionary factors (coordination within groups) may explain the close agreement of perceptive faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'How big is space?' must be qualified
rubrics_metrics.description: 'How big is space?' is meaningless as it stands; 'How big is space for me?' admits of an answer — space is just so large as will suffice to separate all things which coexist for me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that perceptual space has meaning only in relation to groups of sense-impressions and is commensurate with the contents of our perceptive faculty; resist rhetorical appeals to the 'magnitude of space' without clarifying perceptual reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between real (perceptual) and ideal (conceptual) space
rubrics_metrics.description: Space as the order of real coexisting phenomena (real space) is distinct from the space of our thought — the conceptual space of geometry (ideal space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal (conceptual) space may be conceived as finite or infinite and is a product of reasoning, whereas perceptual space is finite and limited by what we perceive to co-exist. Keep conceptual constructions and perceptual experience analytically separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite divisibility is a conceptual limit, not a perceptual fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The limit to the divisibility of space is the limit to our power of perceiving things apart; infinite divisibility belongs to conception, not to perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish Hume's mathematical/mathematical-point arguments: a mathematical point is a conception with no real perceptual existence. Do not conflate imagined unlimited division with perceptual possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions can be valid despite being imperceptible
rubrics_metrics.description: What is imperceptible is not therefore inconceivable; concepts (e.g., circle, point, atom) can be valid even if they have no perceptual counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scientific value of such conceptions lies in their ability to classify, describe, and predict perceptions. Conceptions serve as 'scientific shorthand' enabling economy of thought and useful models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to experience determines perceptual possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Because we conceive a thing, we must not argue that it is possible or probable as a perception; the appeal to experience alone can determine whether a conception is possible as a perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical testing to assess whether a conception corresponds to perceptual reality. Examples: a mathematical point or infinite distance is conceivable but not perceptually real; atoms were treated as conceptual until experiment and observation supported them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sameness and continuity are conceptual ideals, not literal perceptual facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute sameness and continuity are conceptual limits; no two groups of sense-impressions are exactly the same in perceptual experience, and continuity (infinite divisibility preserving 'sameness') is a conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close inspection (microscope, instruments) reveals differences that undermine absolute sameness; physicists and chemists provide arguments that many substances are discontinuous at fine scale. Treat sameness/continuity as useful ideals for classification, not literal facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical definitions are ideal and lack exact perceptual counterparts
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines, planes, curves, and surfaces as defined in geometry are pure conceptions having no correspondence with any possible perceptual experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microscopic inspection shows surfaces and edges to be irregular; geometrical concepts are idealizations used to describe and classify perceptions approximately. Evaluate geometric models by how well they summarize and predict perceptual phenomena, not by literal identity with them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific value judged by classification and predictive power
rubrics_metrics.description: The validity of scientific conceptions depends primarily on the means they provide of classifying and describing perceptions and on their power to codify past and predict future experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if perceptual bodies are not truly spherical or cubical, the concepts of sphere and cube are instrumental if they enable identification, classification, and prediction. Prefer concepts that economize thought and subsume future in their summary of the past.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space as a mode of memory and thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Space as a mode of perception applies as much to memory and to internal impressions as it does to immediate external perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the analogy between external and internal perception; the mode of remembrance is akin to perception though differing in vividness and associative range. This supports localizing psychical processes for a scientific psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unconsciously passing from perception to conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Many paradoxes (e.g., infinite divisibility) arise from an unconscious transition from perceptual limits to conceptual limits and back; we must note when arguments move between imagination and sensory experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about whether claims concern perceptual possibility or conceptual coherence. Critically examine where conceptual operations have been projected onto perception and vice versa (Hume is cited as making such transitions).
